client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup a few months ago. It feels like no matter how hard I work or how many hours I put in, I'm always behind on something — there's always another deadline I'm missing or a project that's slipping. Honestly, I wasn't sure about coming here today because I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change the pile of work waiting for me when I get back.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd question whether being here is worthwhile when the pressure feels so immediate and real — that pile of work isn't going anywhere, and I appreciate you showing up anyway. What you're describing, that feeling of perpetually falling short no matter how much effort you give, sounds genuinely exhausting and demoralizing. I'm curious — when you say you're "always behind," is that a conclusion others at work have expressed to you, or is it more a feeling that lives inside your own head?

client: Honestly, it's mostly inside my own head — my manager hasn't pulled me aside or anything, and I haven't missed any hard deadlines that blew up in my face. But that almost makes it worse, because I can't point to something concrete and say "see, this is proof I'm failing," it's just this constant low-level dread that I'm one bad week away from being exposed as someone who can't actually handle the job. It's like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop.
therapist: What you're describing — that sense of being a fraud who's one misstep away from being "found out" — is something a lot of people experience, and it even has a name: impostor syndrome, which can feel incredibly real even when the external evidence doesn't support it. It's worth noticing that you just gave me some genuinely important data: no missed hard deadlines, no concerned manager, yet your mind is constructing a story of imminent failure anyway. I'm wondering, if a close friend described their situation using exactly the facts you just shared with me, what verdict would you reach about *their* competence?

client: I mean, if a friend told me that, I'd probably say they sound like they're doing fine and just need to cut themselves some slack. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just... doesn't land the same way, it feels like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily or making excuses. I know that probably sounds contradictory, but it's like there are different rules for me than for everyone else.
therapist: You've just noticed something really profound — that you're operating under a double standard where compassion and fair-minded reasoning are available to everyone except yourself, and that's not a contradiction, it's actually one of the most common and painful patterns I see. It's worth gently questioning that rule: where did the idea come from that being kind to yourself is "making excuses," rather than simply being accurate? What do you think it would actually cost you if you held yourself to the same standard you'd apply to a friend?

client: I think part of me genuinely believes that if I ease up on myself, I'll stop pushing as hard and everything will start falling apart — like the self-criticism is actually the thing holding me together and keeping me functional at this job. It's hard to imagine where that came from, but maybe it goes back to always being the "responsible one" growing up, where there wasn't much room to mess up. I guess what it would cost me is this sense of control, even if that control is kind of an illusion.
therapist: You've just made a really meaningful connection — that the self-criticism doesn't feel like cruelty, it feels like *protection*, a coping strategy that may have genuinely served you when you were younger and needed to hold things together. But it's worth examining whether that old strategy is actually delivering what it promises now: you mentioned the control is "kind of an illusion," which suggests some part of you already senses that the harsh self-monitoring isn't truly what's keeping you afloat. What do you think is actually responsible for the real successes you *have* had in this job so far?

client: When I actually stop and think about it, I guess the things that have gone well — like when I got positive feedback on that product presentation last month — came from me genuinely understanding the material and being able to think on my feet, not from beating myself up the night before. But it's uncomfortable to sit with that, because if the self-criticism isn't actually what's making me good at my job, then what's it even for? It's like you're pulling at a thread and I'm not sure I'm ready for what unravels.
therapist: That moment of clarity you just had — recognizing that your real competence came from *you*, your understanding and quick thinking, not from the self-punishment — is genuinely significant, and I want to honor how unsettling it feels to see that. It makes complete sense to feel hesitant, because if the self-criticism isn't the engine driving your success, it means you've been paying a very high emotional price for something that isn't actually protecting you. I'm curious — when you imagine the thread unraveling, what is it you're most afraid you might find underneath?

client: I think what scares me most is finding out that without the self-criticism, there's just... not that much there, like maybe I've been running on anxiety this whole time and if I take that away I'm actually kind of empty or ordinary. It's almost easier to keep the pressure on because at least then I have a reason for why things feel so hard — if I let go of it and still struggle, then I can't blame the anxiety anymore, it's just me. That feels like a much lonelier and scarier conclusion to land on.
therapist: That fear — that without the anxiety there's "not that much there" — is one of the most vulnerable things a person can voice, and I want you to notice that the very way you just articulated it, with that kind of self-awareness and emotional precision, is itself evidence of someone with a great deal *there*. It's also worth gently questioning the logic: you've been running this anxiety-as-fuel experiment for years, and you still can't tell whether it's the anxiety or *you* doing the work, which means you've never actually had a clean look at what you're capable of without it. What might it feel like to run a small experiment — even just for a day — where you tried treating yourself with the same fairness you'd offer a friend, not to "let yourself off the hook," but just to finally get an honest look at what's actually underneath?

client: The idea of even one day without that inner critic running in the background sounds almost foreign to me, and honestly my first instinct is that I'd just spend the whole day waiting for something to go wrong because I wasn't "vigilant" enough. I can see the logic in what you're saying — that I've never actually tested what I'm like without the anxiety — but I'm worried that one bad day during that experiment would just confirm my worst fears rather than disprove them. How do I even know what "treating myself fairly" looks like in practice when I've been doing the opposite for so long?
therapist: That worry about one bad day "confirming your worst fears" is actually really important to examine — because notice that you'd be applying a rule where any struggle becomes proof of failure, but no amount of success counts as proof of capability, which is a game that's impossible to win no matter what happens. As for what "treating yourself fairly" looks like in practice, we don't have to start with a whole day — it could be something as small as noticing one moment where the inner critic fires, pausing, and asking "would I say this to my friend in the same situation?" rather than overhauling everything at once. I'm wondering, is there a specific moment this week — maybe a meeting, a deadline, a piece of work — where you could imagine trying that one small pause as a tiny first experiment?

client: There's actually a sprint review meeting on Thursday where I always end up picking apart everything I present before anyone else even has a chance to respond. I can see how that moment might be a realistic place to try the pause — but I'm a little worried that in the heat of it, when my heart is racing and I'm already in that critical headspace, remembering to stop and ask myself that question is going to feel impossible. It's easy to see the logic right now sitting here, but Thursday-me in that room feels like a completely different person.
therapist: That gap between "therapy-room you" and "Thursday-room you" is completely real, and it's actually wise to plan for it rather than just hoping insight will magically show up under pressure. One thing that can help is creating a tiny, concrete anchor ahead of time — something as simple as writing the question "would I say this to a friend?" on a sticky note in your notebook or as a phone reminder before the meeting, so Thursday-you has a physical prompt rather than relying on memory while your heart is racing. And even if you only catch yourself *after* the self-criticism this time rather than during it, that still counts as the experiment working — so I'm curious, what would it mean to you if Thursday went imperfectly but you noticed the pattern even once?

client: I think if Thursday went badly but I actually caught myself doing it even once, that would genuinely feel like something — like a small crack of light rather than just another meeting I walked out of feeling terrible about myself. But I notice I'm already hedging, already thinking "yeah but what if I don't notice it even once," which is kind of exactly the pattern we've been talking about, isn't it. I guess the sticky note idea feels manageable enough that I don't have a great excuse not to try it, even if part of me is still bracing for it to not work.
therapist: You just caught the pattern in real time, right here in this room — that's not a small thing, that's exactly the muscle you're trying to build for Thursday, and it's already working. I love that you described it as "a crack of light," because that's precisely the right frame: we're not aiming for a transformation, just one small opening that proves the wall isn't as solid as it feels. So you have your experiment, your anchor, and a much more honest picture of what's actually been driving your success — how are you feeling right now compared to when you walked in today?

client: Honestly, I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which I wasn't expecting — I think I came in half-convinced this would just be an hour of talking that changed nothing. There's still a part of me that's skeptical, like I'm worried this feeling won't survive contact with my actual inbox when I get back, but I can at least see that some of what I've been telling myself about the job isn't as solid as it felt two hours ago. I think Thursday is going to be the real test, but for the first time in a while I'm not completely dreading it.
therapist: That shift from dreading Thursday to feeling even cautiously open to it is genuinely meaningful progress, and the skepticism you're holding alongside it is actually healthy — you're not bypassing reality, you're just loosening its grip a little. What you said about the stories you've been telling yourself "not feeling as solid" is exactly what we're working toward, because those stories were never facts, they were just thoughts that went unquestioned for a long time. Before you head back to that inbox, I want to ask — what's one thing you want to remember from today, something you could carry into Thursday that feels true and worth holding onto?
